titleStmt.title: History of the Zhou Dynasty · Shang 商

div.head: c. 1260 BC
div.p: After Pan Geng's death his younger brothers Xiao Xin and Xiao Yi succeeded in turn; by the accession of Xiao Yi's son Wu Ding, the Middle Shang culture had formally passed into Yinxu Phase I.

The main body of the Zhukaigou people left the Ordos region and moved south into northern Shaanxi, exerting a certain influence on the Shang culture of the Guanzhong region; the characteristic Zhukaigou vessel, the snake-pattern li, has been unearthed at Shang-culture sites such as Beicun in Yao County and Yijiabu in Fufeng. Some scholars take them to be the Fang.

During Wu Ding's reign a series of campaigns was also made against the fang states and tribes of the Wei River valley; since the Middle Shang the Shang culture of Guanzhong had taken on an ever more local character, and Wu Ding's dispatch of armies against the Quanfang may be an epitome of the Shang court's attempt to tighten its hold on the western lands once more.

The "Zhoufang" of the oracle-bone inscriptions is generally taken to be the Zhou people who later founded the Zhou dynasty. In the earlier part of King Wu Ding's reign, corresponding in archaeological terms to Yinxu Phase I, the Zhengjiapo culture appeared in the valley of the Qishui River, its sites interspersed with those of the Jingdang-type Shang culture of the Zhouyuan region. At the same time the Sunjia type appeared around Binzhou and Xunyi, close in its cultural character to the Zhengjiapo culture; both have been regarded by scholars as Proto-Zhou culture.

div.head: c. 1260–1235 BC
div.p: The oracle-bone inscriptions show that King Wu Ding of Shang, in the early part of his reign, conquered one after another the Gengfang, Fou, the Jifang, the Jianfang and other states, and gained control of the southern Shanxi region.

Archaeology shows that with the Late Shang Yinxu Phase I the indigenous cultural elements at the Shijia site in Huantai were replaced by Shang culture; the Yinxu oracle-bone inscriptions have a member of the royal clan called Zi Hua, enfeoffed in the east in Wu Ding's first years, whose fief was likewise called Hua. Some scholars hold that Zi Hua was enfeoffed to guard the land the Shang court had newly conquered.

After his campaigns against the fang states of southern Shanxi, Wu Ding went on, with Que, to campaign against the Zhifang and the Peifang; by the inscriptions' description of their position, both bordered the Qiongfang. Yue rose in revolt early in Wu Ding's reign and was likewise put down by Que. After the Zhifang was conquered by the Shang court, its chief Zhi Guo became Wu Ding's vassal, guarding the western frontier for him, sending troops to help him attack the Bafang, and putting down the revolt of the state of Tan in the east.

After this Wu Ding raised a great army and defeated the Qiongfang's ally, the Tufang. Wu Ding's consort Fu Zi was one of the commanders of the campaign against the Tufang; the oracle-bone inscriptions record "calling on Fu Zi to attack the Tufang". Fu Zi is also recorded, in the early part of Wu Ding's reign, as campaigning against the Yifang, the Bafang and other states. Another consort of Wu Ding, Fu Geng, also went out against the Longfang.

Of the fang states that raided the Shang, most raided at widely scattered points but on a small scale each time; not so the Qiongfang, whose raids were frequent and highly destructive, and which often joined with the Tufang to its east in attacking the Shang court. Some scholars connect the Qiongfang with the remains of the Shilou type in archaeological terms, which may have some bearing on its steady extension of its power into the central Shanxi region from the Middle Shang period onward.

After defeating the Tufang, Wu Ding opened his offensive against the Qiongfang; but Fu Zi does not appear in the inscriptions recording that campaign, and some scholars conclude from this that she died after the campaign against the Tufang and before that against the Qiongfang.

On the archaeological level, in Yinxu Phase I the Shang culture of the Hanjiang region was fading away, yet bronze metals from the south still flowed in quantity into the centre of Yin Shang rule, which shows that the Shang court was still at pains to keep indirect control over the peoples of the south; to secure the "copper road", Wu Ding in his reign launched a southern expedition and attacked the Hufang and the Moufang. The Yinxu Phase I inscriptions record Wu Ding and Wang Cheng campaigning against the Moufang, which thereafter appears no more in the inscriptions and is presumed to have been destroyed.

div.head: c. 1260–1235 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Weiyingzi culture developed in succession to the Lower Xiajiadian culture.
The Weifang Phase III culture developed into the Weifang type.

The Miaotaizi type arose; it, the Dachengdun type, the Wucheng culture and other cultures have each been taken by different scholars to be the Hufang. The Lujiahe culture, the Shidiba culture and the Zhouliangyuqiao culture arose.

div.head: c. 1235 BC
div.p: Late Shang culture entered Yinxu Phase II, whose early stage corresponds roughly to the middle and later part of Wu Ding's reign.

From Yinxu Phase II the Liujia culture, regarded by many scholars as the "Qiangfang culture", began a strong rise; its people moved east into the Zhouyuan region, hastening the decline of the Jingdang-type Shang culture.

The Lijiaya culture and the Xicha culture arose; some scholars, from the record in the Zhouyi and the pottery inscriptions unearthed at the Lijiaya site in Qingjian, infer that the Guifang may be the Lijiaya culture.
The Dachengdun type of Late Shang culture gradually went into decline and died out after Pan Geng's move to Yin; the Dachengdun Phase IV culture arose.
As the Weiyingzi culture developed, the Xiaobaiyang type took shape within it.
The Wucheng culture took over from the Shihuishan culture and carried its development forward.

div.head: c. 1230–1150 BC
div.p: The Shang court's war against the Qiongfang went on by fits and starts and dragged out over many years; down to the last years of Wu Ding's reign there are still inscriptions divining about "capturing the Qiongfang" and the like, after which it is no longer seen in the inscriptional record. On the archaeological side, the material remains of the Shilou type suffered heavy damage in Yinxu Phase II: the large rammed-earth buildings at the Gaohong site in Liulin were abandoned, and the type shows a state of decline. These phenomena, it seems, can be connected with Wu Ding's campaigns against the Qiongfang.

After Yinxu Phase II a number of aristocratic tombs of Shang culture, of fairly high rank, appeared in the central Shanxi region; among them, the inscriptions on the bronzes from the Shang tombs at Jingjie in Lingshi and Qiaobei in Fushan have been shown on analysis to belong to the states of Bing and Xian, under the Shang king. Some scholars hold that the Shang king enfeoffed the two states of Bing and Xian to secure the fruits of the victory over the Qiongfang and so keep the north-west stable.

The Heir Apparent Xiao Ji died before Wu Ding. In the texts of the Warring States period he is described as the model of a filial son, and texts from the Han onward enriched the story of Xiao Ji further. On the archaeological side, Xiao Ji is called the "Junior King" in the inscriptions of the early and middle part of Wu Ding's reign; in the late part of Wu Ding's reign Xiao Ji died, a day name was added to his style, and in sacrifice he is called "Junior King Ji".

According to the transmitted texts, Wu Ding was on the throne for as long as fifty-nine years. In his last years Wu Ding prepared to make his youngest son Zu Jia his successor; but Zu Jia held that his elder brother Zu Geng ought by right to succeed, and so, going against his father's command, he fled and hid among the people.

After Wu Ding's death Zu Geng succeeded to the throne without difficulty; he reigned seven years and at his death passed the throne to Zu Jia. In modern times scholars, by ordering and analysing the oracle-bone inscriptions from Yinxu, have found that Zu Jia carried out a series of reforms in his reign, such as establishing the cyclical sacrifice system, simplifying the sacrificial canon and reducing the number of diviners, which strengthened the royal power and secured the political stability of the Shang court.
In the late stage of Yinxu Phase II, Shang culture for the most part withdrew from the western Guanzhong.

div.head: c. 1230–1150 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Misa-ri type reached its lower limit; central-western South Korea entered the stage of Garak-dong, Heunam-ri and Yeoksam-dong. At the same time the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture arose.
The Xujianian site of the Siwa culture appeared.

div.head: c. 1150 BC
div.p: After Zu Jia's death his sons Lin Xin and Kang Ding succeeded in turn. Unlike the relatively peaceful time of Zu Jia, inscriptions concerned with war became frequent again under Lin Xin and Kang Ding. By the accession of Zu Jia's son Lin Xin, the ever-growing Qiangfang had begun to pose a serious threat to the western lands of the Shang court; with the strong eastward advance of the Liujia culture, not only did Shang culture withdraw from the western Guanzhong, but the Zhengjiapo culture, which had only just begun to gather momentum, was hit as well.

Archaeology shows that at the turn from Yinxu Phase II to Phase III, elements of the late Zhukaigou culture and the Lijiaya culture spread south and, blending with the cultures of Guanzhong, formed the remains of the Zaoshugounao type and the Heidouzui type in the Chunhua region. Some scholars think this may be connected with the Fang, grown strong once more in the inscriptions of Lin Xin and Kang Ding; in the inscriptions of Zu Jia's time what concerns war is very little, yet nearly all of it has to do with the raids of the Fang. By the reigns of Lin Xin and Kang Ding its raids, too, had grown more frequent. Other scholars propose to identify it with the "Xunyu Rong and Di" of the transmitted texts, who forced King Tai of Zhou to move south from Bin to Qi Zhou.
The Bronze Age cultures of Qinghai entered the late stage of their middle period; the Upper Zhangjiayuan culture arose.

div.head: c. 1150–1088 BC
div.p: Most of what the Yinxu Phase III inscriptions have on fighting with the Qiangfang belongs to the reign of Kang Ding, younger brother of Lin Xin; unlike those of Wu Ding's time, the inscriptions of Kang Ding's time seldom or never show the choosing of commanders and the levying and mustering of men, and show instead, again and again, the "garrisons" and the "columns" being sent into battle, which reflects an army that by now had a fairly fixed organisation. Besides this, the inscriptions also record Kang Ding calling out dependent tribes and the armies of fang states to attack the Qiangfang.

To judge from what Kang Ding divined about before fighting the Qiangfang, there was no lack of detailed thought on his part about the plan of campaign; on the other hand, these inscriptions also reflect how serious the Qiangfang's raids were, so much so that Kang Ding had to act with caution, and many times called up garrison troops, subject tribes and fang states to reinforce the western lands. Besides the Qiangfang, Kang Ding also had to deal with the raids of the Fang; but in the face of the Fang's raids the measures of the Shang court were mainly defensive, which may be because the chief target at the time was not the Fang but the Qiangfang.

Besides dealing with the Qiangfang and the Fang, Kang Ding in his reign also campaigned against the Weifang in the south-east; in this period the Cuofang, the Peifang, the Xiangfang and the Zifang in the west also gave up the friendly attitude they had kept since Wu Ding's campaigns and turned against the Shang, and Kang Ding was unable to conquer them again.

After Kang Ding's death his son Wu Yi came to the throne; of the western fang states that had raided in Kang Ding's time, the Peifang gave up its hostility and submitted to the Shang court; the Cuofang and the Zifang are not seen in the inscriptions of Wu Yi's time, and what became of them is not known; the Qiangfang and the Xiangfang each have one record in Wu Yi's inscriptions of being attacked by the Shang army, after which the Xiangfang declared its submission.

Another event of some importance in Wu Yi's reign was the migration of the Ji Zhou people; according to the transmitted texts, the Zhou people's former lord Gugong Danfu, who lived at roughly the same time as Wu Yi, was pressed by the "Xunyu Rong and Di" and led his people south from Bin to the Zhouyuan at the foot of Qishan, and after arriving took to wife a woman of the Jiang surname. Danfu led the people in doing away with Rong customs, opened up waste land and built Fortresses and outer walls, and set up the five offices with their officers, bringing the system of government to completion, so that the Zhou people grew stronger day by day. Later ages also honoured Danfu posthumously as King Tai.

Archaeology shows that at the turn from Yinxu Phase II to Phase III the remains of the Nianzipo type and the Sunjia type, distributed on the middle and upper reaches of Jing River, spread south and merged with the Zhengjiapo culture of the Qishui River valley. The Zhengjiapo culture was thereby able to expand rapidly, and developed in convergence with elements of the Liujia culture. As for the Sunjia type that had been in Bin, it was replaced by Duanjing Phase II.

The Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says that King Tai of Zhou had three sons, the eldest Taibo, the second Zhongyong and the youngest Jili, of whom Jili was born of King Tai's principal consort Tai Jiang; the Lienüzhuan, however, holds that Tai Jiang was the mother of all three brothers, Taibo, Zhongyong and Jili. Jili took Tai Ren to wife, and she bore him a son, Chang, who was the later King Wen of Zhou.

By the account of the Shiji, King Tai wished to make Jili his heir so that the throne might pass to Chang, and so Taibo and Zhongyong of their own accord fled to the lands of the barbarians in the south, took "Gouwu" as their style, and founded the state of Wu; some scholars hold that Taibo and Zhongyong did not flee to the lands of the barbarians in the south at all, but led a part of the Zhou people and founded the state of Yu at Pinglu in Shanxi, in order to plan the destruction of Yin Shang. Another group of scholars does not accept this view, and maintains that the place where Taibo and Zhongyong first founded their state was in the Ganjiang valley in Jiangxi, that at the beginning of the Western Zhou they were re-enfeoffed in the Ning–Zhen region of Jiangsu, and that a branch of them was moved back to the Central Plains and separately enfeoffed as the state of Yu.

Some scholars point out that although the inscriptions have no record of direct conflict between Shang and Zhou, some "indirect evidence" can still be found: Wu Yi, for instance, campaigned against the Shaofang of the west, which lay either at Shao Fortress, the fief of Shi, Duke of Shao, in the first years of the Western Zhou, or further north, near the Xiangfang and the Fang.

Besides dealing with the raids of the hostile fang states of the west, the Shang court in this stage also campaigned against the Yifang of the Xu and Huai region; these operations did not match in scale the campaigns of Di Xin's time, but they can still be seen as a foreshadowing of the Shang court's turning the weight of its strategy to the east once more.

Besides this, the northern Shandong region too was a chief area of the Shang court's use of arms in the east at this time; archaeology shows that in the late stage of Yinxu Phase III the range of the Zhenzhumen culture in northern Shandong shrank somewhat, while Shang culture extended east as far as the Mi River valley, of which the Subutun cemetery at Qingzhou is the typical example. Some scholars conjecture that this place is the state of Pugu recorded in the transmitted texts.

Along the Bohai coast, taking in northern Shandong and the eastern part of the Cangzhou region, more than ten clusters of salt-making settlements have been found over a stretch of two hundred and fifty kilometres, each cluster made up of from a dozen or so to several dozen salt workshops, on a grand scale; some scholars hold that the Shang court's management of the east in this stage, and its opening of routes by water and land, were very probably meant to control the sea salt of northern Shandong and to keep the copper and tin of the lower Yangtze moving north without hindrance. It can be seen that when the Shang court of Late Shang Phase III turned the weight of its effort to the east, considerations of economic gain must also have played a part.

Wu Yi, on a hunt in the west, was "struck dead in a thunderstorm"; some scholars think this may be connected with the failure of his western campaign against the Shaofang. After this his son Wen Ding succeeded to the throne.

Although the inscriptions show that Kang Ding and Wu Yi, two generations of Shang kings, had some success in their wars against the hostile fang states of the west, on the archaeological level no strongholds of Shang culture are found reappearing west of Xi'an in the wake of these victories; the Shang cultural elements at the sites of the central Shanxi region likewise faded away by degrees after Yinxu Phase III, while the influence of the Shilou type grew strong again; and it was in just this period that the Zhou people began to extend their sphere of power.

Archaeology shows that after Yinxu Phase III elements of Proto-Zhou culture appear at many sites on the Shanxi–Shaanxi plateau, and spread even as far as the central Shanxi basin. Some scholars think this may be connected with Jili's campaigns against the Rong and Di; of Jili's use of arms along Wei River the transmitted texts have only one record, the destruction of the Bicheng clan. Jili's other recorded campaigns were nearly all directed against the Rong and Di tribes of the Shanxi–Shaanxi plateau.

In the second year of Wen Ding's reign Jili went on with his campaigns against the Di and Rong; using the Gui Rong as a stepping-stone he attacked the Yanjing Rong, but this ended in defeat. Two years later Jili attacked the Rong of Yuwu as well and was victorious, and was appointed mushi by Wen Ding; in the years that followed Jili took the title of King and campaigned again and again against the Rong and Di in the Shanxi region, until at last the Shang court felt threatened, and he was imprisoned by Wen Ding and died.

div.head: c. 1150–1088 BC: archaeological appearances
div.p: The Siwa culture entered the first stage of its middle period, and as it developed the Jiuzhan type took shape within it; the Siwashan type reached its lower limit.
The Shuangfang culture and the Xinchengzi culture took over from the Upper Yujia culture and the Machengzi culture and carried their development forward.
The Sinam-ri Phase II culture and the Geumtan-ri Bronze Age Phase I culture arose.
The Beomui-guseok Phase III culture took over from the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture and carried its development forward.
The Sanxingdui Phase IV culture took over from the Sanxingdui culture and carried its development forward.
The Xindian culture entered its late period.

div.head: c. 1088–1046 BC
div.p: After Jili, King of Zhou, was killed, his son Chang succeeded him as ruler of the state of Zhou; he is King Wen of Zhou. Wen Ding, King of Shang, also died not long after, and his son Di Yi came to the throne; and the Late Shang entered its last phase, Yinxu Phase IV.

The old-text Bamboo Annals records: "Di Yi resided at Yin. In his second year the men of Zhou attacked Shang." Some scholars hold that this shows the conflict between Shang and Zhou sharpening after Jili was killed; as for the outcome of this attack on Shang, the Zhou people's strength was not enough and it cannot have succeeded. And so King Wen of Zhou, after this setback, reviewed his policies at home and abroad afresh, turned to making peace with Yin Shang, and set himself to reversing the balance of strength.

On the archaeological level, after the opening of Yinxu Phase IV Shang culture on the one hand flourished in the east, and on the other dwindled day by day in the west; after the Zhengjiapo culture and the Liujia culture had merged to form the late Proto-Zhou culture of the Qi (岐) and Feng region, the archaeology of the central Shanxi region, once closely tied to Shang culture, likewise shows a blank. In this stage Di Yi campaigned against the Yufang.
The Huaiyi culture took over from the Dachengdun Phase IV culture and carried its development forward.

After Di Yi's death his son Di Xin succeeded to the throne; on the archaeological level, the inscription of the unearthed Zai Hao jiao shows that Di Xin was on the throne for at least twenty-five years, but so far no archaeological evidence has been found of great campaigns against the Dongyi in the last years of Di Xin's rule. In the early and middle part of Di Xin's reign, however, there are indeed oracle-bone inscriptions on campaigning against the Yifang, and records in bronze inscriptions that bear on it.

Of Di Xin's military operations against the Yifang, the best known is the "campaign against the Yifang in the tenth si", carried out after more than a year of planning and preparation; the inscription of Jiawu of September in Di Xin's tenth si shows Di Xin preparing to campaign against the Yifang together with Xi, Marquis of the state of You, which lay close to the Yifang, and holding, before setting out, a rite of announcement sacrifice in the royal domain, at the "Great Settlement Shang".

In November of the tenth si Di Xin reached Wei (危). At the beginning of December he joined forces with Xi, Marquis of You, and from the day Guiyou began fighting the Yifang. By the record of the inscriptions, ten days later the Yifang seems for a time to have fallen back. After that Di Xin led his army to the banks of Huai River and conquered the Linfang; on Bingwu of January the Shang army fought the Yifang again. After the victory Di Xin, in February of the eleventh si, set out from You on the road home and brought his army back.
Note: the "Huai" (淮) of the line of march can also be read as "Wei" (潍), so that there are two accounts.

Besides the "campaign against the Yifang in the tenth si", Di Xin also launched a "campaign against the Yifang in the fifteenth si"; the evidence comes from the inscription of the rhinoceros zun of the Lesser Minister Yu, of the end of Shang: "The King bestowed on the Lesser Minister Yu cowries of Kui. It was when the King came back from campaigning against the Yifang; it was the King's fifteenth si, the day of the rong sacrifice." Several further oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions of the end of Shang, their year and month unknown, also bear on the campaigns against the Yifang.

While using arms abroad, Di Xin also strengthened the royal power at home, strictly keeping up the "cyclical sacrifice system" of sacrifices to the former kings and their consorts; compared with the other former kings who kept the cyclical sacrifice system, Di Xin, in order to concentrate the royal power, carried the suppression of the collateral branches of the royal clan from the level of sacrifice over to the level of politics, made ever greater use of Lesser Ministers and kept the old nobility at a distance, as is borne out by the Huang-group inscriptions, in which the employment of Lesser Ministers on affairs outweighs the offices of the old nobility. In this way the balance long kept in the politics of the Shang was broken, the established institutions of the Shang court ceased to run smoothly, and the stability of the political system was undermined.

In addition, Di Xin took in many fugitives from every quarter, which sharpened his conflicts with the clans and the fang states; King Wen of Zhou did the opposite, and expressly put forward the policy "Make great inquisition for fugitives", that is, to hunt down fugitives and send them back to their masters, by which he won over the clans within Yin Shang and its dependent fang states.

According to the transmitted texts, while the state of Zhou was thriving, Chang, King of Zhou, was lured, seized and imprisoned at Youli by Di Xin. Later, after seven years of bribes and gifts from the ministers of Zhou, King Wen was at last released to return to his state, and was appointed "Chief of the West" by Di Xin.

According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou, a dispute arose between the two states of Yu (虞) and Rui, neither of which would give way, and so they went to King Wen of Zhou for a ruling. When the rulers of the two states arrived in Zhou and saw that the ways of the people prized courtesy and yielding, they went home ashamed and contended no more. The matter soon spread abroad, and the Lords all said: "The Chief of the West must be the ruler who has received the Mandate!" Some scholars hold that King Wen's settling of the "suit of Yu and Rui" was a means of rousing his kinsmen and allied states and of spreading abroad the talk of his "receiving the Mandate".

According to the Yi Zhou Shu, Awakening at Cheng, King Wen, because of a strange dream of his consort Tai Si, held a rite to avert calamity and, with the Heir Apparent Fa, "bowed and received the auspicious dream", to show that he had received from the "August High God" the Mandate of Heaven that had been Yin Shang's; the Zhou people therefore regarded this year as the "year of receiving the Mandate". History records that in the "year of receiving the Mandate" King Wen settled the "suit of Yu and Rui", in the second year attacked the Quan Rong, in the third year attacked Mixu, and in the year after destroying Mixu attacked the state of Qi (耆). After attacking Qi, King Wen went on to attack Yu (邘), cutting off the natural barrier on the west of the royal domain of Yin Shang.

The conflict between the old nobility of Yin Shang and Di Xin grew sharper by the day, and Di Xin, busy forcing the nobles at home into submission, was perhaps for the time unable to respond to what the Zhou people were doing; the many dependent states of Yin Shang in the Shanxi region, the state of Lü and others, also went over to the Zhou people at about this time.

King Wen of Zhou's next aim was to open the main road to the east and sweep away the state of Chong; the Laoniupo site in Baqiao District, Xi'an, is held by some scholars to belong to the state of Chong, and by the results of radiocarbon dating the site was abandoned about the end of Shang; the medium-sized tombs with wooden chambers within the site were badly wrecked, not one being spared, the remains of the tomb occupants were thrown out, and of the grave goods eight or nine parts in ten are gone. This was perhaps an act of revenge by the Zhou people on Hu, Marquis of Chong, and his clan.

According to the Rongchengshi of the Shanghai Museum Chu slips, the states subdued by King Wen also included Feng, Hao, Nuo, Lu and others; Yi River, Luo River and the western Henan region were brought into King Wen of Zhou's sphere of power at about this time. When this series of campaigns was over King Wen of Zhou moved his capital to the settlement of Feng, and died the year after. After King Wen of Zhou's death the Heir Apparent Fa succeeded to the throne; he is King Wu of Zhou.

According to the transmitted texts, some years after coming to the throne King Wu raised a great army to attack Shang, carrying King Wen's spirit tablet and declaring that he marched at his father's command, and sent men to bring the clans and tribes of every region together for a review of arms at Meng Ford; some scholars hold that King Wen died seven years after receiving the Mandate, and that King Wu went on with the count of years from the Mandate and never began a count of his own. Reckoned in this way, the "ninth year" of the review of arms at Meng Ford in the Shiji is in fact the second year of King Wu's reign. Another group of scholars takes the opposite view, pointing out that the pre-Qin texts record King Wu as having a count of years of his own, such as a "first si".

On the view that "King Wu began a count of his own", fully nine years passed from King Wu's accession to the review of arms at Meng Ford, and in this time the Zhou people slackened the continuous expansion of King Wen's later years and turned to the ordering of the settlement of Feng and the building of Haojing; as for the Shang, with the power of the Zhou people already pressing on the royal domain, Di Xin, even though he had the disaffection of his kinsmen and the old clans at home to deal with, had no choice but to free his hands and take countermeasures against the Zhou people.

The "review of Li" mentioned in the Zuozhuan was perhaps the military disposition Di Xin made in answer to the Zhou state's offensive; Di Xin moved his army up to the state of Qi (Li), held a review of troops and organised manoeuvres, and by this show of force brought the state of Qi back over to Yin Shang.

If the "review of Li" of the Zuozhuan is accepted, then "the Dongyi revolted from him" that follows it should likewise have happened in the later part of Di Xin's rule; the archaeological evidence shows that several undated bronze inscriptions on "campaigning against the Yifang" do not rule out the possibility that the war between Shang and the Yifang went on to Di Xin's twenty-first si or even later. If the above inference holds, then the revolt of the Dongyi, coming not long after the "review of Li", very probably upset Di Xin's plans, so that he could do nothing further to remove the threat of the Zhou people's power to the royal domain.

On the other side, the Zhou people for their part were not willing to lose control of the state of Li, and so, once their internal consolidation was complete and their preparations fully made, the Zhou people campaigned against the state of Li a second time and put it down at one stroke; the Qiye of the Tsinghua slips records: "In King Wu's eighth year he campaigned against Qi and greatly conquered it."

According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou: when King Wu reviewed his arms at Meng Ford, "the Lords who met at Meng Ford without appointment were eight hundred"; the Lords who took part in the meeting one after another demanded that Zhou (纣) be attacked and Shang destroyed at once, and King Wu said to them: "You do not yet know the Mandate of Heaven; it cannot be done yet." And with that he led his army back; some scholars hold that this "review of arms at Meng Ford" of King Wu's was in the nature of a manoeuvre, to learn the road and the ground, so that in future he could use Luoshi as a forward base and cross the river northwards without difficulty.

According to the transmitted texts, not long after King Wu's "review of arms at Meng Ford" a grave split appeared within the ruling group of Yin Shang. To hold down the nobles who opposed him, Di Xin took very extreme measures; the final outcome was that Prince Bigan was killed, Jizi was imprisoned, and the Grand Preceptor Ci, the Junior Preceptor Qiang and others went straight over to the state of Zhou. King Wu judged that the time was ripe, and proclaimed to the allied Lords: "Yin has committed grave crimes; it cannot but be attacked to the end!"

On Guisi of January in King Wu's eleventh year the Zhou army formally set out, with three hundred war chariots, three thousand Tiger Braves and forty-five thousand armoured men; the armies of the allied fang states came to join the Zhou army, and King Wu made the Great Declaration to address the Lords and all the gentlemen. After crossing the Yellow River on the day Wuwu, the Zhou army reached Muye, outside Zhaoge, the secondary capital of Yin Shang, in the night of Guihai of February; according to the Guoyu, Discourses of Zhou, rain fell in the night of Guihai and the Zhou army drew up its lines in the rain, and at daybreak the next day, Jiazi, King Wu made the Speech at Mu before the lines, proclaiming Di Xin's crimes.

By the account of the Yi Zhou Shu, Conquest of Yin, in the battle of Muye Di Xin's army was broken by the charge of the picked troops of Zhou and was defeated, and Di Xin burned himself to death on Lu Terrace on the evening of that same day, Jiazi; there is also an account that Di Xin was taken alive and then beheaded.
